title.en: The Bowl That Measured the Rain

summaryEn: Hoya follows the Joseon crown prince's rain experiments to the 1442 rain gauge, the cheugugi, and meets the only Joseon rain-gauge vessel known to survive.
learningGoalsEn: Read and recognize 비 (bi, rain) and the short sentence 비가 와요 (biga wayo, It's raining).
Know that a 1441 royal record describes the crown prince (later King Munjong) testing rain with a metal vessel, and that the device was named 측우기 (cheugugi, rain gauge) in 1442.
Understand that officials measured rain with a standard ruler and kept written records across the provinces.
Know that the only Joseon rain gauge vessel known to survive was made in 1837 and is a National Treasure.

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

scenes.narrationEn: Pitter-patter! Hoya the tiger holds out a paw to catch the raindrops. "In Korean, rain is {kw:bi}," he says. "Long ago, the Joseon kingdom found a clever way to measure rain. Let's go and see!"
scenes.artBrief: A small, friendly tiger cub in a light vest stands in gentle rain holding out one paw; soft gray clouds and a tiled-roof Korean house behind him.

scenes.narrationEn: A royal record from 1441 says the crown prince, the king's son who later became King Munjong, worried about drought. After each rain, he dug into the ground to see how deep the water had soaked in.
scenes.captionEn: The crown prince digs to check the rain
scenes.artBrief: A young Joseon crown prince in a red robe kneels in a palace garden beside a small hole, looking at damp soil; a dry field in the distance.

scenes.narrationEn: But soil can be dry or damp, so digging could not show exactly how much rain had fallen. Instead, he had a copper vessel made and placed in the palace to collect the rainwater.
scenes.captionEn: A copper vessel collects the rain
scenes.artBrief: A plain metal cylinder standing in a palace courtyard catching rain, while the prince watches from under the wooden eaves.

scenes.narrationEn: In 1442, in King Sejong's reign, a standard rain gauge was named {kw:cheugugi}, 'rain-measuring device.' It stood on a stand at the royal observatory office. After each rain, an official measured the water with a standard ruler and wrote it down.
scenes.captionEn: An official measures rain with a ruler
scenes.artBrief: A Joseon official in a black hat dips a slim wooden ruler into a metal rain gauge on a square stone stand; a brush and a record book lie beside him.

scenes.narrationEn: Rain gauges and rulers were sent to every province. Local towns could make their gauges from pottery, set them on a stand in a courtyard, measure each rain, and report it to the king.
scenes.captionEn: Rain gauges are sent to every province
scenes.artBrief: A pottery rain gauge on a stone stand in a country government courtyard; a local magistrate measures with a bamboo ruler; green hills behind.

scenes.narrationEn: Joseon sent rain gauges across the land, but only one gauge itself is known to survive today: the rain gauge of the Chungcheong provincial office in Gongju. It was made of bronze in 1837 and is a National Treasure.
scenes.captionEn: Only one Joseon gauge vessel is known to survive
scenes.artBrief: A bronze cylindrical rain gauge made of three stacked sections, displayed on a museum pedestal under a soft spotlight; Hoya gazes up in wonder.

scenes.narrationEn: Today it is kept at the National Meteorological Museum of Korea in Seoul. Hoya grins and points at the sky. "Next time it rains, you will know the words: {kw:biga-wayo}!"
scenes.captionEn: The gauge rests in a museum in Seoul
scenes.artBrief: Hoya under a small paper umbrella, pointing happily at the rainy sky in front of a modest museum building.

checks.promptEn: Why wasn't digging in the soil good enough to measure rain?

options.en: Rain never soaked into the soil at all
Soil can be dry or damp, so the exact amount stayed unclear
The crown prince was not allowed to dig

checks.explainEn: Soil can be dry or damp, so digging could not show exactly how much rain had fallen.

options.en: The speed of the wind outside
The warmth of the air at noon
The amount of rain that falls

checks.explainEn: A cheugugi collected rainwater, and an official measured how deep the water was with a standard ruler.

checks.promptEn: When was the surviving Gongju rain gauge made?
checks.explainEn: The Gongju rain gauge was made of bronze in 1837. It is the only Joseon gauge vessel known to survive.

facts.claimEn: A Sejong Sillok entry dated 1441 (Sejong year 23, 4th lunar month, 29th day) records that the crown prince, worried about drought, used to dig into the ground after rain to see how far the water had soaked in, and because this did not show the exact amount, had a vessel cast from copper (銅) and placed in the palace to measure the rainwater it collected. The crown prince at that time later became King Munjong.
facts.claimKo: 『세종실록』 세종 23년(1441) 4월 29일 기사에 따르면, 세자는 가뭄을 걱정하여 비가 온 뒤마다 땅을 파서 빗물이 스며든 정도를 살폈으나 정확히 알 수 없었으므로, 구리를 부어 그릇을 만들어 궁중에 두고 그릇에 고인 빗물의 양을 재어 보았다. 이 세자는 훗날의 문종이다.

sources.title: 세종실록 92권, 세종 23년(1441) 4월 29일 을미 1번째 기사 「황우의 변에 대해 승정원에 전지하다」
sources.quoteOrLocator: 국역: "근년 이래로 세자가 가뭄을 근심하여, 비가 올 때마다 젖어 들어 간 푼수[分數]를 땅을 파고 보았었다. 그러나 적확하게 비가 온 푼수를 알지 못하였으므로, 구리를 부어 그릇을 만들고는 궁중(宮中)에 두어 빗물이 그릇에 괴인 푼수를 실험하였는데" / 원문: 世子憂旱, 每當雨後, 入土分數, 掘地見之。然未可的知分數, 故鑄銅爲器, 置於宮中

sources.title: 통영 측우대
sources.quoteOrLocator: 내용: "측우기의 제도는 1441년(세종 23)에 당시 왕세자였던 문종의 주도하에 만들어졌지만 임진왜란 이후 그 제도가 쇠잔해졌다가"

facts.claimEn: A Sejong Sillok record of a Ministry of Revenue (Hojo) proposal states that soil differs in dryness and dampness, so the depth to which rain soaks into the ground is hard to know.
facts.claimKo: 『세종실록』에 실린 호조의 건의에 따르면, 흙의 마르고 젖은 정도가 같지 않아 빗물이 흙 속으로 스며든 깊이를 알기 어렵다.

sources.title: 세종실록 93권, 세종 23년(1441) 8월 18일 임오 4번째 기사 「호조에서 서운관에 측우기를 설치할 것을 건의하다」
sources.quoteOrLocator: 국역: "토성(土性)의 조습(燥濕)이 같지 아니하고, 흙속으로 스며 든 천심(淺深)도 역시 알기 어렵사오니, 청하옵건대, 서운관(書雲觀)에 대(臺)를 짓고 쇠로 그릇을 부어 만들되 … 대(臺) 위에 올려 놓고 비를 받아"

sources.title: 6) 측우기의 발명과 농업기상학의 발달 (신편 한국사 27권 조선 초기의 문화 Ⅱ > Ⅰ. 과학 > 2. 천문 기상학)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "빗물이 땅 속에 스며드는 깊이는 땅이 말랐을 때와 젖었을 때에 따라서 차이가 심하게 드러나기 때문이다."

facts.claimEn: In 1442 (Sejong year 24), a cast-metal instrument was named 측우기 (cheugugi, 'rain-measuring instrument'). In the capital it was placed on a stand at the Seoun-gwan (the royal office for astronomy and weather), and after each rain an official measured the water depth with a standard ruler (jucheok) and recorded it.
facts.claimKo: 1442년(세종 24) 쇠로 주조한 기구에 측우기라는 이름을 붙였다. 서울에서는 서운관에 대를 만들어 측우기를 그 위에 두고, 비가 온 뒤마다 관원이 주척으로 물의 깊이를 재어 기록하였다.

sources.title: 세종실록 96권, 세종 24년(1442) 5월 8일 정묘 1번째 기사 「호조에서 우량을 측정하는 일에 관해 아뢰다」
sources.quoteOrLocator: 국역: "서울에서는 쇠를 주조(鑄造)하여 기구(器具)를 만들어 명칭을 측우기(測雨器)라 하니 … 서운관(書雲觀)에 대(臺)를 만들어 측우기를 대(臺) 위에 두고 매양 비가 온 후에는 본관(本觀)의 관원이 친히 비가 내린 상황을 보고는, 주척(周尺)으로써 물의 깊고 얕은 것을 측량하여 … 상세히 써서 … 기록해 둘 것이며"

sources.title: 국보 공주 충청감영 측우기 (Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "1442년(세종 24)에 발명된 측우기는 … 땅에 스며든 물의 깊이를 측정하던 이전의 비합리적인 강우 측정방식에서 벗어나 본격적으로 강수량을 정량적으로 측정 가능케 한 발명품"

facts.claimEn: Cast-metal rain gauges and standard rulers were sent from the capital to each province; local offices could make gauges of porcelain or earthenware, place them on a stand in the courtyard of the official guesthouse (gaeksa), and the magistrate measured each rain, reported it to the king and kept a record.
facts.claimKo: 중앙에서 쇠로 주조한 측우기와 주척을 각 도에 보냈고, 각 고을은 자기나 와기로 측우기를 구워 만들어 객사 뜰의 대 위에 두었으며, 수령이 비가 온 뒤 물의 깊이를 재어 임금에게 보고하고 기록하였다.

sources.title: 세종실록 96권, 세종 24년(1442) 5월 8일 정묘 1번째 기사 「호조에서 우량을 측정하는 일에 관해 아뢰다」
sources.quoteOrLocator: 국역: "외방(外方)에서는 쇠로써 주조(鑄造)한 측우기(測雨器)와 주척(周尺) 매 1건(件)을 각도(各道)에 보내어, 각 고을로 하여금 … 혹은 자기(磁器)든지 혹은 와기(瓦器)든지 적당한 데에 따라 구워 만들고, 객사(客舍)의 뜰 가운데에 대(臺)를 만들어 측우기를 대(臺) 위에 두도록 하며 … 수령(守令)이 친히 … 계문(啓聞)하고 기록해 두어서"

sources.title: 국보 공주 충청감영 측우기 (Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "조선시대에는 중앙정부에서 측우기를 제작해 전국의 감영에 보냈기 때문에 여러 점이 만들어졌으리라 예상되지만, 지금까지 ‘공주 충청감영 측우기’만 유일하게 알려져 있다."

sources.title: 공주 충청감영 측우기
sources.quoteOrLocator: "조선 세종 때 반포되고 영조 때 개정된 우량 관측제도에 의하면, 전국 팔도의 감영(監營)에 측우기를 설치하여 강우량을 측정, 보고하도록 했다."

facts.claimEn: The Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju (공주 충청감영 측우기), made of bronze in 1837 (Heonjong year 3), is the only Joseon-period rain gauge vessel known to survive, and it is designated a National Treasure. (Several stone bases/stands on which gauges were set also survive, but no other gauge vessel.)
facts.claimKo: 공주 충청감영 측우기는 1837년(헌종 3)에 청동으로 만든 것으로, 현재까지 알려진 유일한 조선시대 측우기(빗물을 받는 그릇)이며 국보로 지정되어 있다. 측우기를 올려 두던 대석(臺石)은 몇 기가 남아 있다.

sources.title: 국보 공주 충청감영 측우기 (Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "국보 ‘공주 충청감영 측우기(公州 忠淸監營 測雨器)’는 1837년(헌종 3)에 제작된 것으로, 측우대는 없고 측우기만 전해오고 있다. … 지금까지 ‘공주 충청감영 측우기’만 유일하게 알려져 있다." / 지정일 2020.02.27

sources.title: 공주 충청감영 측우기
sources.quoteOrLocator: "청동으로 제작된 이 측우기는 표면에 새겨진 “도광정유제(道光丁酉製)”라는 글귀를 통해 1837년(헌종 3)에 제작되었음을 알 수 있다." / "빗물을 담는 그릇으로 현존하는 것은 금영 측우기가 유일하다." / 종목: 국보(2020년 02월 27일 지정) / 현황: "측우기를 설치했던 대석(臺石)은 몇 기가 남아 있지만" (the page continues that the vessel survives only as the 금영 측우기).

sources.title: 통영 측우대
sources.quoteOrLocator: 정의: "19세기 경상도 통영에 위치한 수군통제영에서 설치하였던 측우기 받침대." / "2010년 보물로 지정되었다." (a surviving stone stand, showing that stands survive although gauge vessels do not)

facts.claimEn: The Rain Gauge of Chungcheong Provincial Office, Gongju is kept at the National Meteorological Museum of Korea (국립기상박물관) in Jongno-gu, Seoul.
facts.claimKo: 공주 충청감영 측우기는 서울 종로구의 국립기상박물관에 있다.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. All quotes re-checked programmatically against fetched pages (Sillok, encykorea, 우리역사넷, NMK, KMA; KHS descriptions via the khs.go.kr open API SearchKindOpenapiDt.do?ccbaCpno=...). unesco.org/ich.unesco.org pages could not be fetched directly (connection reset); UNESCO wording and years (2009, 2013, 2018) confirmed from search excerpts of the UNESCO pages and KHS lists. Corrections: Heo Jun birth year dropped from narration/fact (sources conflict: 1539 vs 1546, encykorea internally inconsistent); Jang Yeong-sil rank sentence softened to match the Sillok ('decided to give'); 우리역사넷 added as second source for Donguibogam f4/f5; Ssirum UNESCO locator de-quoted.

authorNotes: Attribution: popular retellings often say Jang Yeong-sil invented the rain gauge, but the Sejong Sillok (1441-04-29, lunar) credits the crown prince's (later King Munjong's) experiments and encykorea's 통영 측우대 entry says the system was made under the crown prince's lead; Jang Yeong-sil is therefore not mentioned. Deliberately omitted: the KHS description's comparative claim that the cheugugi was the world's first scientific rain gauge, about 200 years before the West (priority claims are contested); the 1441-08-18 proposal's dimensions and the 1442 standard size (1 cheok 5 chon by 7 chon); the Gongju gauge's removal to Japan (KHS: c.1915; encykorea: early 1910s) and return in 1971 (colonial-era history is out of scope); the 1770/1771 revival under King Yeongjo (sources differ on the year). Materials: the Sillok uses 銅 (copper/bronze) for the crown prince's 1441 vessel and 鐵 (cast metal/iron) for the 1442 standard, so narration says 'copper' and 'metal' respectively; the Gongju gauge is bronze (encykorea). All Sillok dates are lunar. Theme set to 'crafts' to match BP04/BP05 Pillar E (E3 측우기). REVISION: (a) Scene 6/summary/learning goal now say only one gauge VESSEL survives; stone stands (대석/측우대) also survive (encykorea E0007902; Tongyeong stand is a Treasure, E0068941). (b) Museum English name 'National Meteorological Museum of Korea' taken from the museum's own website footer (science.kma.go.kr/museum/); the KHS portal lists only the Korean name. (c) Romanization of 서운관 is Seoun-gwan (seo-un-gwan); 'Seounwan' (proposed by one fact-check) would transcribe 서운완, so it was not adopted. (d) Second source added for f2 (신편한국사 via 우리역사넷); new sources accessed 2026-10-10. PR 1.8c: check c1 distractors replaced with options the story contradicts (s2: the water soaked in; the crown prince dug), so the item has one answer from the story text.
